clean_title: AnyFlow: an on-policy distillation framework for any-step video diffusion
summary:
🚀 We are excited to announce the release of AnyFlow, the first any-step video diffusion on-policy distillation (OPD) framework. By leveraging Flow Map distillation, AnyFlow significantly enhances model inference efficiency by reducing sample steps. (Code, models, and demos are now open-source!)
Key Highlights:
⚡ Any-Step Generation: Unlike traditional distilled models tied to fixed step budgets, AnyFlow enables a single model to adapt to arbitrary inference budgets. It achieves high-quality few-step generation while providing stable improvements as more sampling steps are added.
🔀 Multiple Architectures: AnyFlow supports any-step distillation for both causal and bidirectional video diffusion models.
🎬 Multiple Tasks: AnyFlow supports Text-to-Video, Image-to-Video, and Video-to-Video generation within one causal video diffusion model.
📈 Scalable Performance: AnyFlow is validated from 1.3B up to 14B parameters.

Validated on models from 1.3B to 14B parameters, AnyFlow enables flexible and scalable video generation. Code, models, and demos are available online.

clean_title: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
summary:
Want to better understand Gated DeltaNet?
Find it here, alongside the 153 papers which cite it:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJE6PSRX0AAXXnd.jpg
Quoting @ahatamiz1
Gated DeltaNet-2 is here. 🚀
🔥 New paper: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
Gated DeltaNet-2 outperforms KDA and Mamba-3, the latest and best recurrent architectures, head to head at 1.3B. 🏆
💡 Here's the idea behind it:
Linear attention squeezes an unbounded KV cache into a fixed-size recurrent state. The hard part isn't just what to forget, it's how to edit that memory without scrambling the associations already in it.
Prior delta-rule models like Gated DeltaNet and KDA use one scalar gate to do two jobs at once: erasing old content and writing new content. But these two decisions act on different axes of the state, so tying them together is a real limitation.
Gated DeltaNet-2 decouples them.
✂️ a channel-wise erase gate b_t picks which key-side coordinates to read and remove
✍️ a channel-wise write gate w_t picks which value-side coordinates to commit
🔁 recovers KDA when both gates collapse to a scalar, and Gated DeltaNet when the decay collapses too
⚡ still trains fast: chunkwise WY algorithm with gate-aware backward, fused in Triton
📊 Results:
We train 1.3B models on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu, matched in recurrent state size, against Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, and Mamba-3.
Best average on language modeling + commonsense reasoning, in both recurrent and hybrid settings
Biggest gains on long-context RULER retrieval. S-NIAH-3 jumps from 63 to 90 over KDA, and multi-key needle retrieval climbs from 28 to 38
Joint work with @YejinChoinka and @jankautz.
📄 Paper:
💻 Code:
#LinearAttention #StateSpaceModels #Mamba #LLM
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI4EF-va8AAhlVe.jpg
clean_summary:
Gated DeltaNet-2 improves linear attention by decoupling the erase and write operations, addressing a limitation in prior models where a single scalar gate handled both tasks. It uses channel-wise gates to selectively erase old memory and write new content, leading to better performance on language modeling and long-context retrieval tasks.

Experiments with 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens show that Gated DeltaNet-2 outperforms recent architectures like KDA and Mamba-3, especially in long-context retrieval scenarios. The model maintains fast training speed through a chunkwise WY algorithm with gate-aware backward pass, and achieves significant gains in tasks like RULER retrieval and multi-key needle retrieval.

The stage between pre-training and post-training
A base model is continued on a smaller, curated data mixture chosen to strengthen capabilities that the original pre-training run undercovered, such as multilinguality, domain knowledge, or long-context extension.
It usually keeps a pre-training-like objective, but uses higher-quality or more targeted data so later instruction tuning, preference tuning, or RL can shape behavior on top of stronger capabilities.

clean_title: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference with DFlash and V2
summary:
What is speculative decoding?
Speculative decoding is an inference optimization that uses a fast, small "draft" model to quickly propose several future tokens, which are then verified in parallel by a larger, slower "target" model.
This process significantly speeds up the token generation of large language models (LLMs) by allowing the generation of multiple tokens per step, without sacrificing the quality of the output text
Learn more at
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HK318caXsAIqDLk.jpg
Quoting @lmsysorg
🚀 New blog: The next generation of speculative decoding: DFlash and Spec V2
DFlash + Spec V2 hit >4.3X baseline throughput for LLM inference, now the default speculative decoding engine in SGLang! Together with @modal and our jointly-released DFlash drafter for Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B beats both baseline and native MTP in every setting we benchmarked:
1️⃣ >4.3X baseline & 1.5X native MTP throughput (concurrency 1, HumanEval, 8xB200)
2️⃣ Block diffusion drafter: a full token block in one forward pass
3️⃣ KV injection: target-model features fed into every draft layer’s KV cache for higher acceptance
4️⃣ Spec V2 overlap scheduler: +33% end-to-end
Read the code, deploy a DFlash server, and start experimenting!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HK3hNFMbQAA5kLl.jpg
clean_summary:
Speculative decoding is an inference optimization that uses a small, fast draft model to propose multiple future tokens, which are then verified by a larger, slower target model. This approach significantly increases the speed of token generation in large language models by allowing multiple tokens to be generated per step without reducing output quality.

A new blog introduces DFlash and Spec V2, which achieve over 4.3 times the baseline throughput for LLM inference and are now the default in SGLang. These innovations include block diffusion for full token blocks in one pass, KV injection for higher acceptance, and an overlap scheduler that improves end-to-end performance by 33%. The code is available for deployment and experimentation.

This work addresses the challenge of synthesizing a novel-view video from a monocular reference video along a target camera trajectory, which requires maintaining geometric consistency and motion fidelity. Existing methods based on explicit 3D representations are limited by the accuracy of off-the-shelf 3D models.

MVTrack4Gen introduces a multi-view point tracking approach that serves as geometric supervision to improve 4D video generation. The method leverages geometric cues to enhance the quality of the synthesized videos, ensuring better consistency and realism. The project includes an implementation available on GitHub and has been featured on Paper with Code, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating high-quality 4D videos from monocular inputs.

clean_title: DanceOPD: On-Policy Generative Field Distillation for Multi-Capability Image Generation
summary:
🎨 𝗗𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗢𝗣𝗗: 𝗢𝗻-𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
We explore how to compose diverse generation and editing abilities into a single unified model.
Project:
Paper:
Modern image generation models are increasingly expected to support many capabilities at once: T2I, local editing, global editing, realism enhancement, and guidance absorption.
Yet these abilities often interfere with each other. For example, improving editing may hurt the original T2I quality, while local and global editing may pull the model toward different behaviors.
DanceOPD views each capability as a velocity field in a shared flow-matching state space, and distills them into one student model through hard-routed on-policy field matching.
Across T2I + editing, local + global editing, realism-field absorption, and CFG absorption, DanceOPD improves multi-capability composition while preserving strong anchor generation quality.
#GenerativeAI #DiffusionModels #OPD #FlowMatching #AIGC
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2070366038198460416/img/DkBNN_LtuTqDrl7l.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2070366038198460416/vid/avc1/360x270/x66lfJTkMljvUJwA.mp4?tag=28
clean_summary: DanceOPD explores how to combine diverse image generation and editing abilities into a single unified model. Modern image generation models are expected to support many capabilities such as text-to-image, local and global editing, realism enhancement, and guidance absorption, but these abilities often interfere with each other. DanceOPD views each capability as a velocity field in a shared flow-matching state space and distills them into one student model through on-policy field matching. This approach improves the composition of multiple capabilities while maintaining strong image generation quality, enabling models to perform various tasks simultaneously without sacrificing performance.

clean_summary: Lilian Weng's blog has been added as a recommended read to the Scaling Laws method on Papers with Code. The post discusses the importance of scaling laws in deep learning, which describe how training loss decreases predictably as model size, dataset size, and compute increase, following a power-law relationship. It explains how scaling laws help estimate the optimal compute allocation between data and model size before large-scale experiments, addresses disagreements between Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla, and highlights the challenges of extrapolation due to data limits and fitting details.

linked_urls.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully | Lil'Log
linked_urls.summary: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

clean_summary:
Visual generative models are usually trained in two separate stages: first, a tokenizer is trained for reconstruction and then frozen, followed by training a generator on its discrete indices or continuous latents. This separation prevents the tokenizer from being aware of what the generator learns.

The referenced work introduces GEAR, a method that aims to unify these stages into an end-to-end process, potentially improving the coherence and quality of generated images. Supporting resources include a GEAR tokenizer collection and the GitHub repository for Tencent-Hunyuan's GEAR implementation.

clean_title: Outstanding ICML paper studies the phenomenon of Grokking
summary:
One of the Outstanding Papers at ICML studies the phenomenon of Grokking.
What is Grokking? It is a training phenomenon in which a model abruptly transitions from overfitting (high training accuracy, poor held-out performance) to generalizing after many optimization steps with little or no test improvement, unlike the gradual co-improvement usually seen in machine learning.
The term was introduced by OpenAI in 2022 on small algorithmic tasks such as modular arithmetic, and follow-up work interprets grokking as a phase transition during training, often linked to weight decay, optimizer dynamics, and a shift from lazy to rich learning regimes..
Learn more about it here, as well as all 188 papers which study it:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMofl5TXIAA9XnM.jpg
Quoting @icmlconf
🏆Announcing the #ICML2026 Awards! 🏆
Including Outstanding Papers (research paper & position paper, winner & honorable mentions) and the Test of Time Award!
Check out the blog post for all winners (or read on), laudatio, & description of the processes.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMf33L0aoAAL_v0.jpg
clean_summary: One of the outstanding papers at ICML explores Grokking, a training phenomenon where a model suddenly shifts from overfitting—high training accuracy but poor test performance—to generalizing well after many optimization steps with little or no test improvement. The term was introduced by OpenAI in 2022 on small algorithmic tasks like modular arithmetic, and subsequent work interprets grokking as a phase transition during training, often related to weight decay, optimizer dynamics, and a shift from lazy to rich learning regimes. This research helps understand how models learn and generalize in unexpected ways.

clean_summary:
SAM2Matting reaches new state-of-the-art performance on video matting benchmarks such as VideoMatte240K. It upgrades foundation video trackers like SAM2 into advanced image and video matting models by decoupling temporal tracking from fine-grained alpha estimation, enabling zero-shot video matting without video training.

The work addresses the challenge of video matting, which involves both high-level tracking and low-level detail extraction. The approach leverages the strengths of foundation models to improve accuracy and generalization in video matting tasks.

title: DailyPapers (@HuggingPapers)
clean_title: Large-scale distillation attack on the Kimi K3 technical report
summary:
We ran a large-scale distillation attack on the Kimi K3 technical report by reading it in parallel at the Hugging Face Journal Club :)
Our main takeaway is that there doesn't appear to be any "secret sauce" behind frontier performance.
Instead, K3 is a demonstration of how many difficult algorithmic and infrastructure decisions have to work together (distillation, RL scheduling, environments, quantisation, MoE sharding etc) to push a model to the frontier.
Here’s what we learned:
• Frontier post-training increasingly looks like expert training followed by distillation. K3 trains specialists across three domains and three reasoning-effort levels, then distils the resulting nine experts back into a single checkpoint using multi-teacher OPD
• Reasoning effort is treated as a trainable capability. Token budgets are estimated from the SFT model, and a stage-wise curriculum anneals from long to short rollouts to produce low-, high- and max-effort experts.
• Partial rollouts keep expensive RL infrastructure busy. Completed trajectories can trigger immediate updates, while unfinished ones are carried into later iterations and reprioritised through a priority queue. Per-token corrections help control the resulting off-policy behaviour.
• The reward model is itself an agent. Rather than relying only on fixed or binary rewards, it generates task-specific rubrics and scores responses against them on the fly.
• The environment interface is designed for composition. A unified, white-box abstraction allows the same training system to operate across different agent harnesses like Codex, CC, Hermes instead of specialising around a single one.
• The systems work is as interesting as the algorithmic work. GPUs dynamically switch between training and inference, rollout concurrency responds to KV-cache pressure, and reference models can live on CPU until needed.
• Quantisation is part of training—not merely deployment. K3 uses QAT for weights and activations, while matching the trainer and inference server’s quantisation schemes to reduce train–inference mismatch.
• The chat template is novel and introduces an extensible token markup language is intended to accommodate new tools and modalities without repeatedly redesigning the template.
• Synthetic task generation is becoming increasingly autonomous. Agents traverse a knowledge graph and search the web to generate training tasks at scale, although the report leaves some details of their integration underspecified. (This part was very cool)
clean_summary:
A large-scale distillation attack was conducted on the Kimi K3 technical report during the Hugging Face Journal Club. The main insight is that frontier performance does not rely on a secret sauce but results from many complex algorithmic and infrastructure choices working together, including distillation, RL scheduling, environments, quantisation, and MoE sharding.

Key lessons include that post-training frontier models resemble expert training followed by distillation, with specialists across domains and reasoning levels combined into a single checkpoint. Reasoning effort is treated as a trainable capability, with curriculum annealing from long to short rollouts. Partial rollouts keep RL infrastructure busy, with trajectories being reprioritised and corrected to manage off-policy effects.

The reward model acts as an agent, generating task-specific rubrics and scoring responses dynamically. The environment interface is designed for composition across different agent harnesses, and systems adaptively switch between training and inference on GPUs. Quantisation is integrated into training via QAT to reduce mismatch, and a novel chat template introduces an extensible token markup language for future tools and modalities. Lastly, synthetic task generation is becoming more autonomous, with agents traversing knowledge graphs and searching the web to create training data at scale.

💻 Meet Qwen-CUA — our native computer-use agent for (almost) everything.
Code, APIs, and computer use are three of the most important interfaces for agents. Today’s models are already highly capable with the first two. Qwen-CUA is built to unlock the third: graphical interfaces designed for people.
👀 Native Perception — screenshots only. No DOM, accessibility tree, or other hidden machine-readable state.
🖱️ Native Interaction — keyboard and mouse events across browsers, desktop apps, and professional software. No task-specific APIs.
🧠 Native Intelligence — maintains long-horizon visual context, verifies progress, and learns from large-scale interactive experience with verifiable outcomes.
To make native computer use trainable at scale, we built approximately 40K verifiable tasks and rollout infrastructure with nearly 100K vCPUs, supporting tens of thousands of concurrent environments.
Across eight computer-use benchmarks spanning everyday desktop use, long-horizon workflows, personalized computing, scientific research, web interaction, macOS, and adversarial robustness, Qwen-CUA demonstrates strong and broadly competitive capabilities. Scaling the same recipe to Qwen-CUA-Max pushes this frontier further.
Not just “clicking the screen” — native computer use unlocks software and workflows that previously required a human at the keyboard. Together with code and APIs, it completes the interface stack for more general agents.
Joint work by Qwen Team × XLang Lab.

title: DailyPapers (@HuggingPapers)
clean_title: A joint scaling law for pretraining and RL
summary:
📈 A joint scaling law for pretraining and RL
We read a very interesting paper in the HF journal club today: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
The authors use chess as a controlled environment to sweep compute across pretraining, SFT, and RL to derive a joint pretraining–RL scaling law:
R(C_RL, N, T) = f(L_pt(N, T)) + g(N, T) × log(C_RL / C_ref)
Here, N is model size, T is the number of pretraining tokens, and C_RL is the compute spent on RL.
→ The main insight is that stronger pretraining makes RL itself scale better, with the pretraining loss determining the perf that can be reached at a given RL budget.
→ The optimal compute split changes with scale. At low total budgets, pretraining dominates because weaker policies benefit less from RL. As the budget grows, the compute-optimal allocation shifts toward RL, rising from roughly 20% to 28% across the range studied.
→ RL improves reliability more than coverage. It produces strong improvements in pass@1, but much smaller and less consistent gains in pass@k. On easy puzzles, RL mostly amplifies correct moves already preferred by the SFT model. On harder puzzles, it can surface correct moves from the low-probability tail, but also reinforces incorrect moves.
Initially I was sceptical about chess as the main domain, but the authors observe the same qualitative pattern across checkpoints of a 1B language model trained on math - neat!
For me the main practical question is whether a similar scaling law would hold for mid-training + RL, which is far more common than training everything from scratch 🤔
clean_summary: A recent paper discussed in the Hugging Face journal club explores how pretraining and reinforcement learning (RL) scale together using chess as a controlled environment. The authors derive a mathematical relationship showing that stronger pretraining improves the efficiency of RL, with the pretraining loss setting an upper bound on achievable performance given an RL compute budget. They find that at small compute budgets, pretraining dominates, but as the budget increases, more resources should be allocated to RL, rising from about 20% to 28%. RL tends to enhance reliability more than coverage, improving pass@1 significantly but with smaller gains in pass@k, especially on harder puzzles where it can both surface correct moves and reinforce mistakes. Although initially skeptical about chess as a domain, the authors observe similar scaling patterns in models trained on math data, suggesting broader applicability. A key question remains whether similar laws apply during mid-training combined with RL, which is more common in practice.

summary:
🚀 We release CLR, the test-time scaling method previously used in VibeThinker-3B.
CLR is built on a simple idea that solving and falsification have asymmetric capability requirements. With the same model, establishing a correct solution through forward reasoning is harder than falsifying one decisive wrong claim.
Rather than verifying entire solutions, CLR focuses on decision-critical claims and suppresses unreliable reasoning—compressing the survival space of incorrect traces and allowing more reliable ones to emerge.
🔥 On GPT-OSS-20B, when a correct trace is already present but standard self-consistency still fails, CLR rescues ~37% of such cases on average.

clean_title: MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences
summary:
Introducing MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences 📱🧠
Paper:
Code:
Dataset:
Website:
Long-term memory is essential for personalized AI agents. Yet most existing benchmarks reduce a user to a sequence of conversations.
Real life is far more complex.
Personal knowledge is scattered across calendars, notes, bills, to-do lists, screenshots, photos, and app interactions in the realistic mobile environment. It evolves over time, and critical evidence may be buried among millions of tokens of distractors.
MobileMem brings memory evaluation closer to this reality.
We introduce a benchmark for testing whether agents can organize, update, retrieve, and reason over year-scale, cross-application mobile experiences.
⚡ What MobileMem offers:
📱 Mobile Memory Evaluation
A trajectory in MobileMem contains heterogeneous experiences across diverse applications.
🧭 Knowledge-Guided Experience Synthesis
Our KEME framework transforms fragmented sessions into temporally coherent, continually evolving user trajectories through top-down planning and bottom-up experience updates.
📝 Text + Multimodal Tracks
The text track uses a predefined protocol for apps to send records as structured text events, while the multimodal track models non-integrated apps where assistants learn from user-shared screenshots.
🧠 Comprehensive Memory Tasks
The MobileMem benchmark suite includes diverse question types, such as multi-hop retrieval, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, relationship and preference understanding, visual reasoning, abstention, and more.
🔍 What did we discover?
• Better retrieval does not always mean better memory: stronger systems may retrieve weakly related evidence and become more confidently wrong on unanswerable questions.
• Converting images into captions is not enough. Captions improve visual reasoning by 3.50%, but reduce performance on other questions by 4.43% because of memory interference.
• Controlled experiments suggest that well-designed distractors can be more challenging than simply extending trajectory's length.
MobileMem reveals that future memory systems must do more than store additional information.
They must update outdated knowledge, distinguish evidence from interference, reason across time and modalities, and know when not to answer.
#MobileMem #LLM #Agent #Memory #MultimodalAI #Benchmark #NLP
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HP5dCjPa4AA4-kB.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HP5dCi-bMAAp2X0.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HP5dCi9bAAAluwq.jpg

clean_summary:
MobileMem introduces a benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents can organize, update, retrieve, and reason over year-scale, cross-application mobile experiences. It reflects the complexity of real life, where personal knowledge is scattered across calendars, notes, bills, screenshots, and app interactions, evolving over time and buried among distractors.

The benchmark includes heterogeneous experiences across diverse apps, with a framework that transforms fragmented sessions into coherent user trajectories through top-down planning and experience updates. It features text and multimodal tracks, modeling structured text events and shared screenshots, and includes tasks like multi-hop retrieval, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and visual reasoning.

Findings reveal that better retrieval does not always improve memory, as systems may retrieve weakly related evidence and become confidently wrong. Converting images into captions helps visual reasoning but can reduce performance on other tasks due to memory interference. Controlled experiments show that challenging distractors can be more difficult than longer trajectories. Overall, future memory systems must do more than store information—they need to update outdated knowledge, distinguish evidence from interference, reason across modalities and time, and recognize when not to answer.

linked_urls.summary: Computer Use Agents are AI systems that can interact with computer interfaces, understand graphical user interfaces, execute tasks, and navigate software applications autonomously. These agents combine vision, language understanding, and action planning to perform complex computer-based tasks. Current directions include: **Native visual policies are replacing stitched agent stacks.** The frontier is moving from DOM/accessibility-tree pipelines and prompt-engineered wrappers toward end-to-end vision-language-action models that unify screenshot perception, GUI grounding, deliberative planning, memory, and cross-platform action spaces. [Aguvis](/paper/2412.04454), [UI-TARS](/paper/2501.12326), and [Mobile-Agent-v3.5](/paper/2602.16855) trace this shift from pure-vision interaction to one policy spanning desktop, mobile, and web.; **Grounding is becoming an active inference process.** High-resolution professional interfaces expose the limits of one-shot coordinate prediction, so leading systems increasingly zoom, crop, verify, or invoke tools before clicking. On [ScreenSpot-Pro](/benchmark/screenspot-pro?task=computer-use-agents), two-stage refinement in [Mobile-Agent-v3.5](/paper/2602.16855) and [MAI-UI](/paper/2512.22047) yields large gains, showing that adaptive visual search can matter as much as larger backbones.; **Executable environments are turning interaction data into a flywheel.** Progress is shifting from static imitation on scarce human traces to synthetic task generation, stateful rollouts, multi-turn reinforcement learning, and verifiable rewards. [UI-TARS-2](/paper/2509.02544) stabilizes long-horizon RL in unified sandboxes, while [Fara-1.5](/paper/2606.20785) and [CUA-Gym](/paper/2605.25624) scale environment generation and automated verification, making coverage and reward fidelity the main training frontier.
